claim: CaMKII is an oligomeric enzyme with crucial roles in neuronal signaling and cardiac function.
source: Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) is an oligomeric enzyme with crucial roles in neuronal signaling and cardiac function.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about CaMKII supported by scientific consensus and citations in the manuscript.

claim: Activation of CaMKII triggers the exchange of subunits between holoenzymes.
source: Previously, we showed that activation of CaMKII triggers the exchange of subunits between holoenzymes, potentially increasing the spread of the active state (Stratton et al., 2014; Bhattacharyya et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Unphosphorylated peptides derived from the CaMKII-α regulatory segment bind to the CaMKII-α hub and break it into smaller oligomers.
source: Using mass spectrometry, we show now that unphosphorylated and phosphorylated peptides derived from the CaMKII-α regulatory segment bind to the CaMKII-α hub and break it into smaller oligomers.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study supported by mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Phosphorylated peptides derived from the CaMKII-α regulatory segment bind to the CaMKII-α hub and break it into smaller oligomers.
source: Using mass spectrometry, we show now that unphosphorylated and phosphorylated peptides derived from the CaMKII-α regulatory segment bind to the CaMKII-α hub and break it into smaller oligomers.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study supported by mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Regulatory segments dock spontaneously at the interface between hub subunits in molecular dynamics simulations.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations show that the regulatory segments dock spontaneously at the interface between hub subunits, trapping large fluctuations in hub structure.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Regulatory segment docking traps large fluctuations in hub structure.
source: Molecular dynamics simulations show that the regulatory segments dock spontaneously at the interface between hub subunits, trapping large fluctuations in hub structure.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Activation of CaMKII-α results in the destabilization of the holoenzyme.
source: Single-molecule fluorescence intensity analysis of CaMKII-α expressed in mammalian cells shows that activation of CaMKII-α results in the destabilization of the holoenzyme.
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule TIRF microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Release of the regulatory segment by activation and phosphorylation allows it to destabilize the hub, producing smaller assemblies that might reassemble to form new holoenzymes.
source: Our results suggest that release of the regulatory segment by activation and phosphorylation allows it to destabilize the hub, producing smaller assemblies that might reassemble to form new holoenzymes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Each subunit of CaMKII has an N-terminal kinase domain that is followed by a regulatory segment and an unstructured linker that leads into a C-terminal hub domain.
source: Each subunit of CaMKII has an N-terminal kinase domain that is followed by a regulatory segment and an unstructured linker that leads into a C-terminal hub domain (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CaMKII structure, supported by the figure and scientific consensus.

claim: The regulatory segment blocks the substrate-binding site of the kinase in the autoinhibited state of CaMKII.
source: The regulatory segment blocks the substrate-binding site of the kinase in the autoinhibited state of CaMKII (Rosenberg et al., 2005; Rellos et al., 2010), and this inhibition is released by the binding of Ca2+/calmodulin (Ca2+/CaM) to a calmodulin-binding element within the regulatory segment (Figure 1B; Ikura et al., 1992; Meador et al., 1992; Meador et al., 1993; Rellos et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural and biochemical studies.

claim: Inhibition of the kinase is released by the binding of Ca2+/calmodulin to a calmodulin-binding element within the regulatory segment.
source: The regulatory segment blocks the substrate-binding site of the kinase in the autoinhibited state of CaMKII (Rosenberg et al., 2005; Rellos et al., 2010), and this inhibition is released by the binding of Ca2+/calmodulin (Ca2+/CaM) to a calmodulin-binding element within the regulatory segment (Figure 1B; Ikura et al., 1992; Meador et al., 1992; Meador et al., 1993; Rellos et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural and biochemical studies.

claim: The hub domains of CaMKII associate to form a ring-shaped scaffold containing twelve or fourteen subunits.
source: The hub domains of CaMKII associate to form a ring-shaped scaffold containing twelve or fourteen subunits, around which the kinase domains are arranged (Figure 1A; Hoelz et al., 2003; Rellos et al., 2010; Chao et al., 2011; Myers et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies and the figure showing the architecture.

claim: Mutations in CaMKII affect learning and memory formation in mice.
source: Mutations in CaMKII affect learning and memory formation in mice (Silva et al., 1992; Giese et al., 1998; Elgersma et al., 2002), and mutations in human CaMKII have been identified in patients with cognitive and developmental impediments (Robison, 2014; Küry et al., 2017; Chia et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies in mice.

claim: Mutations in human CaMKII have been identified in patients with cognitive and developmental impediments.
source: Mutations in CaMKII affect learning and memory formation in mice (Silva et al., 1992; Giese et al., 1998; Elgersma et al., 2002), and mutations in human CaMKII have been identified in patients with cognitive and developmental impediments (Robison, 2014; Küry et al., 2017; Chia et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous clinical studies.

claim: Two samples of CaMKII labeled separately with fluorophores of two different colors showed activation-dependent co-localization when mixed and activated.
source: This conclusion was based on the results of experiments in which two samples of CaMKII were labeled separately with fluorophores of two different colors, mixed, and then activated. Single-molecule visualization showed activation-dependent co-localization of the two fluorophores (Stratton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Mixing CaMKII samples labeled with FRET donor and acceptor fluorophore pairs after activation led to increased FRET compared to mixing unactivated samples.
source: In other experiments, separate CaMKII samples were labeled with FRET donor and acceptor fluorophore pairs, respectively, and mixing these samples after activation led to increased FRET compared to mixing unactivated samples (Bhattacharyya et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Activated CaMKII holoenzymes could phosphorylate subunits of unactivated ones, thereby spreading the activation signal.
source: Importantly, these experiments showed that activated CaMKII holoenzymes could phosphorylate subunits of unactivated ones, thereby spreading the activation signal (Stratton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The regulatory segment of CaMKII has been shown to be important for subunit exchange.
source: The regulatory segment of CaMKII has been shown to be important for subunit exchange (Stratton et al., 2014; Bhattacharyya et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Autophosphorylation of Thr 286 in the regulatory segment prevents it from re-binding to the kinase domain, thereby conferring Ca2+/CaM independence (autonomy) on CaMKII.
source: After activation, autophosphorylation of Thr 286 in the regulatory segment prevents it from re-binding to the kinase domain, thereby conferring Ca2+/CaM independence (autonomy) on CaMKII (Miller et al., 1988; Thiel et al., 1988; Lou and Schulman, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous biochemical studies.

claim: Autophosphorylation of Thr 305 and Thr 306 prevents the binding of Ca2+/CaM to the regulatory segment.
source: Autophosphorylation of two other sites, Thr 305 and Thr 306, prevents the binding of Ca2+/CaM to the regulatory segment (Colbran, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Activation is accompanied by the release of at least some fraction of the regulatory segment from the kinase and from Ca2+/CaM.
source: Thus, we expect that activation is accompanied by the release of at least some fraction of the regulatory segment from the kinase and from Ca2+/CaM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phosphorylation data and known biochemical properties.

claim: A constitutively active variant of CaMKII-α (T286D) undergoes spontaneous subunit exchange without activation by Ca2+/CaM.
source: A constitutively active variant of CaMKII-α (T286D) undergoes spontaneous subunit exchange without activation by Ca2+/CaM (Stratton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Mutation of the calmodulin-binding element of the regulatory segment in the T286D variant eliminated subunit exchange.
source: Mutation of the calmodulin-binding element of the regulatory segment in this variant eliminated subunit exchange, which suggests that the calmodulin-binding element might interact with the hub and destabilize it, thereby promoting subunit exchange (Stratton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The calmodulin-binding element might interact with the hub and destabilize it, thereby promoting subunit exchange.
source: Mutation of the calmodulin-binding element of the regulatory segment in this variant eliminated subunit exchange, which suggests that the calmodulin-binding element might interact with the hub and destabilize it, thereby promoting subunit exchange (Stratton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the mutation data.

claim: A construct consisting of just the hub and the regulatory segment was shown to undergo spontaneous subunit exchange.
source: Consistent with this, a construct consisting of just the hub and the regulatory segment was shown to undergo spontaneous subunit exchange (Bhattacharyya et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: While the isolated hub is very stable, the holoenzyme, especially with the linker present, is unstable and undergoes dissociation.
source: Recent differential scanning calorimetry and mass photometry experiments have shown that while the isolated hub is very stable, the holoenzyme, especially with the linker present, is unstable and undergoes dissociation (Torres-Ocampo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: The hub assembly has grooves located at the inter-subunit interfaces that are lined by negatively-charged residues.
source: A prominent feature of the hub assembly is the presence of grooves located at the inter-subunit interfaces. These grooves are lined by negatively-charged residues, and we proposed that positively-charged residues in the calmodulin-binding element might recognize these negatively-charged residues (Bhattacharyya et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on structural observations and previous work by the authors.

claim: Positively-charged residues in the calmodulin-binding element might recognize negatively-charged residues in the interfacial grooves.
source: A prominent feature of the hub assembly is the presence of grooves located at the inter-subunit interfaces. These grooves are lined by negatively-charged residues, and we proposed that positively-charged residues in the calmodulin-binding element might recognize these negatively-charged residues (Bhattacharyya et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on structural features.

claim: Each interfacial groove between subunits contains the uncapped edge of a β-sheet.
source: Each interfacial groove between subunits contains the uncapped edge of a β-sheet, and peptide segments have been shown to dock within the groove by forming an additional strand of this β-sheet (Chao et al., 2011; Bhattacharyya et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Peptide segments have been shown to dock within the interfacial groove by forming an additional strand of the β-sheet.
source: Each interfacial groove between subunits contains the uncapped edge of a β-sheet, and peptide segments have been shown to dock within the groove by forming an additional strand of this β-sheet (Chao et al., 2011; Bhattacharyya et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: A peptide with the sequence of the calmodulin-binding element has been shown to bind weakly to the hub, with a dissociation constant of ~90 µM.
source: A peptide with the sequence of the calmodulin-binding element has been shown to bind weakly to the hub, with a dissociation constant of ~90 µM, but destabilization of the hub was not studied in those experiments (Bhattacharyya et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The isolated hub without added peptides shows a distribution of ions corresponding to dodecameric and tetradecameric hub assemblies in mass spectrometry.
source: The mass spectrum of the CaMKII-α hub without added peptides is shown in Figure 2A. We observe a distribution of ions only in the higher m/z range, which correspond to dodecameric and tetradecameric hub assemblies.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Under soft ionization conditions (cone voltage of 50 V), no smaller oligomeric species are observed for the isolated hub.
source: In the present study, we used softer ionization conditions, with a cone voltage of 50 V. Although this results in a decrease in the mass spectral resolution, we do not observe any smaller oligomeric species for the isolated hub.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Addition of 100 µM of Peptide A to the hub leads to the release of monomers, dimers, tetramers and hexamers within less than 3 min.
source: In the presence of 100 µM of Peptide A, we observe hub species comprised of dodecamers and tetradecamers, as well as new species corresponding in mass to the intact complex with a peptide adducted. In addition, smaller oligomeric species that correspond to monomers, dimers, tetramers and hexamers of hub subunits appear within less than 3 min (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: After 4 min of incubation with 100 µM of Peptide A, smaller oligomeric species are predominant.
source: After 4 min, these smaller species are predominant.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Incubation of the hub with Peptide A at 10 µM concentration yields release of smaller oligomeric species within ~ 1–2 min.
source: Incubation of the hub with Peptide A at 10 µM concentration also yields spectra that demonstrate the release of smaller oligomeric species within ~ 1–2 min, although the peptide is sub-stoichiometric with respect to the hub under this mixing condition (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: At 1 µM concentration of Peptide A, there is essentially no disassembly of the hub, even after ~10 min.
source: At even lower concentrations (1 µM) of Peptide A, we see essentially no disassembly of the hub, even after ~10 min, although there is some hexamer present at levels that are marginally above the noise.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Incubation at saturating concentrations of peptide (1 mM) yields very noisy spectra with a high baseline consistent with significant protein/peptide aggregation.
source: Incubation at saturating concentrations of peptide (1 mM) yields very noisy spectra with a high baseline consistent with significant protein/peptide aggregation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Incubation of the hub with 100 µM of Peptide B causes disassembly of the hub and the release of monomers, dimers, tetramers and hexamers, but at a slower rate than seen with Peptide A.
source: The incubation of the hub with 100 µM of Peptide B also causes disassembly of the hub and the release of monomers, dimers, tetramers and hexamers, but at a slower rate than seen with Peptide A.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Addition of 1 mM of Peptide C to the hub did not cause hub disassembly.
source: Peptide B does not contain the positively charged residues of the calmodulin-binding element. To test the importance of positive charge in Peptide A, we replaced three positively charged residues with glutamate (Peptide C, see Figure 1B). Addition of 1 mM of Peptide C to the hub did not cause hub disassembly (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Peptide C fails to bind to the hub.
source: These results are in agreement with previously reported binding measurements that showed that this peptide fails to bind to the hub (Bhattacharyya et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Incubation of the hub with 1 mM of Peptide D does not result in the release of smaller oligomeric species after 8 min.
source: The results of the incubation with 1 mM of Peptide D, where the entire β-clip segment is replaced with glycine and serine residues, are shown in Figure 3C. Only intact dodecamers and tetradecamers are observed after 8 min.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Peptides E and F, in which only portions of the β-clip segment are replaced by glycine and serine residues, cause hub disassembly but to a lesser extent than Peptide A at similar peptide concentrations.
source: Peptides E and F, in which only portions of the β-clip segment are replaced by glycine and serine residues, cause hub disassembly (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,1B) but to a lesser extent than Peptide A at similar peptide concentrations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,1B.

claim: Peptide G (containing the autonomy site) does not induce hub disassembly.
source: We also tested the effect of two control peptides that are known to interact with the kinase domain but are not known to bind to the hub. The first (Peptide G, Figure 1B) contains the autonomy site (Thr 286) of the regulatory segment (Lou and Schulman, 1989), and the second, CaMKIINtide (Peptide H, Figure 1B), is an inhibitor that binds to the substrate recognition site of the kinase domain (Chang et al., 1998; Chao et al., 2010). Some adduction of these peptides to the intact complexes is observed, but neither peptide induces hub disassembly (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C ), pointing to a specific role for the calmodulin-binding element in disturbing the integrity of the CaMKII-α hub.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: CaMKIINtide (Peptide H) does not induce hub disassembly.
source: We also tested the effect of two control peptides that are known to interact with the kinase domain but are not known to bind to the hub. The first (Peptide G, Figure 1B) contains the autonomy site (Thr 286) of the regulatory segment (Lou and Schulman, 1989), and the second, CaMKIINtide (Peptide H, Figure 1B), is an inhibitor that binds to the substrate recognition site of the kinase domain (Chang et al., 1998; Chao et al., 2010). Some adduction of these peptides to the intact complexes is observed, but neither peptide induces hub disassembly (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C ), pointing to a specific role for the calmodulin-binding element in disturbing the integrity of the CaMKII-α hub.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The calmodulin-binding element has a specific role in disturbing the integrity of the CaMKII-α hub.
source: Some adduction of these peptides to the intact complexes is observed, but neither peptide induces hub disassembly (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C ), pointing to a specific role for the calmodulin-binding element in disturbing the integrity of the CaMKII-α hub.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of different peptides on hub stability.

claim: Phosphorylation at Thr 305 and Thr 306 prevents rebinding of Ca2+/CaM to the holoenzyme.
source: The calmodulin-binding element contains two residues, Thr 305 and Thr 306, that can be phosphorylated when CaMKII is activated, and phosphorylation at these sites prevents rebinding of Ca2+/CaM to the holoenzyme (Colbran, 1993; Bhattacharyya et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The breakage of the hub is accelerated in the presence of the phosphorylated peptide compared to the unphosphorylated peptide.
source: In these experiments, CaMKII-α hub at a final subunit concentration of 120 µM was incubated with Peptide Aphos for 5 min at room temperature prior to injection into the mass spectrometer under similar ionization conditions as before. Under these conditions, the mass spectra obtained comprised predominantly of smaller oligomeric species and aggregates, suggesting that the breakage of the hub is accelerated in the presence of the phosphorylated peptide compared to the unphosphorylated peptide.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: At higher peptide concentrations of 100 µM and 10 µM of Peptide Aphos, smaller oligomeric species appear within ~1 min.
source: At the higher peptide concentrations of 100 µM and 10 µM of Peptide Aphos, smaller oligomeric species appear within ~1 min (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: At a lower concentration of 1 µM of Peptide Aphos, smaller oligomeric species do not appear until ~2 min after ionization.
source: At a lower concentration of 1 µM of Peptide Aphos, smaller oligomeric species do not appear until ~2 min after ionization Figure 4C.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: When the hub is mixed with 100 µM of Peptide Bphos, smaller oligomeric species are observed within a minute.
source: We also tested the stability of the hub (120 µM final subunit concentration) when mixed with 100 µM of Peptide Bphos, again with no pre-incubation of the peptide with the hub, and observed smaller oligomeric species within a minute (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Phosphorylated versions of the regulatory segments are more effective at destabilizing the hub than the unphosphorylated species.
source: The data show that phosphorylated versions of the regulatory segments are more effective at destabilizing the hub than the unphosphorylated species (compare the data shown in Figures 2 and 3A with the data in Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of mass spectrometry data across multiple figures.

claim: The phosphorylated and unphosphorylated peptides bind to the hub with comparable affinity.
source: This result is unexpected, since the phosphorylated and unphosphorylated peptides bind to the hub with comparable affinity (Bhattacharyya et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Gel filtration analysis of the CaMKII hub incubated with Peptide A shows only a single protein peak corresponding to dodecameric/tetradecameric species.
source: For example, gel filtration analysis of the CaMKII hub incubated with Peptide A under conditions identical to those used for mass spectrometry shows only a single protein peak corresponding to dodecameric/tetradecameric species (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the gel filtration data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gel filtration causes dissociation of the peptide from the hub, perhaps allowing the hub to reassemble.
source: Since Peptide A interacts with the hub relatively weakly (Bhattacharyya et al., 2016), it is possible that gel filtration causes dissociation of the peptide from the hub, perhaps allowing the hub to reassemble.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the discrepancy between gel filtration and mass spectrometry results.

claim: Perturbations introduced by the mass spectrometric analysis, such as sample heating, might partially destabilize the hub making it possible to more readily observe the effects of the peptides on the hub stability.
source: In addition, perturbations introduced by the mass spectrometric analysis, such as sample heating, might partially destabilize the hub making it possible to more readily observe the effects of the peptides on the hub stability.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for why mass spectrometry detects hub destabilization.

claim: Two of the twelve regulatory segments dock on the hub in the 13 µs molecular dynamics simulation.
source: In the simulation with the regulatory segments present, two of the twelve regulatory segments dock on the hub (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The regulatory segment of subunit L docks at the interface between subunits B and L within 0.5 µs.
source: The regulatory segment of subunit L docks within 0.5 µs (hereafter referred to as Docking 1), and that of subunit F docks at ~3 µs (referred to as Docking 2) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The regulatory segment of subunit F docks at the interface between subunits F and H at ~3 µs.
source: The regulatory segment of subunit L docks within 0.5 µs (hereafter referred to as Docking 1), and that of subunit F docks at ~3 µs (referred to as Docking 2) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The docking involves hydrogen-bond formation between the calmodulin-binding element (residues 292–310) and the open edge of the β-sheet (residues 410–416) located at the interface.
source: The docking involves hydrogen-bond formation between the calmodulin-binding element (residues 292–310) and the open edge of the β-sheet (residues 410–416) located at the interface (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,2B).
evidence: This is supported by the molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,2B.

claim: Both docking events are initiated by interactions between positively-charged residues on the regulatory segments and negatively-charged residues that line the interfacial groove.
source: Both docking events are initiated by interactions between positively-charged residues on the regulatory segments and negatively-charged residues that line the interfacial groove (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), although there are differences in the specific interactions that are made and in the register of the regulatory segments within the interfacial grooves.
evidence: This is supported by the molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Backbone hydrogen bonds are formed between the regulatory segment and the β-sheet at the interface, leading to the incorporation of this portion of the regulatory segment into the β-sheet.
source: Backbone hydrogen bonds are then formed between the regulatory segment and the β-sheet at the interface, leading to the incorporation of this portion of the regulatory segment into the β-sheet, similar to the β-clip (Chao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the molecular dynamics simulation data and comparison to previous structural work.

claim: The hydrophobic sidechains of the β-clip segment pack into the hydrophobic core of the subunits, further stabilizing docking by the regulatory segment.
source: The hydrophobic sidechains of the β-clip segment pack into the hydrophobic core of the subunits, further stabilizing docking by the regulatory segment.
evidence: This is supported by the molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The backbone hydrogen bonds between the regulatory segment and the β-sheet are stable and persist for the duration of the simulation.
source: Unlike the electrostatic interactions, which are transient, the backbone hydrogen bonds are stable and persist for the duration of the simulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The interfaces at which two dockings occur are located diametrically across from each other on the hub.
source: The interfaces at which two dockings occur are located diametrically across from each other on the hub (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and docking is accompanied by a large conformational change at both interfaces (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Docking is accompanied by a large conformational change at both interfaces.
source: The interfaces at which two dockings occur are located diametrically across from each other on the hub (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and docking is accompanied by a large conformational change at both interfaces (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The core structures of the individual subunits remain relatively unchanged over the course of the simulation.
source: The core structures of the individual subunits remain relatively unchanged over the course of the simulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), allowing us to use the angle between the axes of the αA helices as a measure of the overall rotation of one subunit at an interface with respect to the other.
evidence: This is supported by the molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The angle between the αA helices of subunits B and L increases from ~50° to ~60° when Docking 1 is initiated, then to ~80° where it remains for the rest of the trajectory.
source: The initial value of the inter-helix angle between the αA helices of subunits B and L, which bracket the interface at which Docking 1 occurs, is ~50°. These subunits begin to rotate away from each other when the trajectory is initiated, and the angle between helices αA has increased to ~60° when Docking 1 is initiated (Figure 6C). At this point, there is a marked increase in the angle between the αA helices (to ~80°), where it remains for the rest of the trajectory (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by the molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: During the course of the simulation, the hub distorts from its normal circular shape to an oval shape, but it does not actually separate at any of the interfaces.
source: During the course of the simulation, the hub distorts from its normal circular shape to an oval shape, but it does not actually separate at any of the interfaces (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B D).
evidence: This is supported by the molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,D.

claim: The large distortions at the two docking interfaces are compensated for by closure of the remaining interfaces.
source: This is because the large distortions at the two docking interfaces are compensated for by closure of the remaining interfaces (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Hydrogen bonds across the subunit interfaces are maintained, irrespective of whether an interface opens or closes.
source: Hydrogen bonds across the subunit interfaces are maintained, irrespective of whether an interface opens or closes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B D).
evidence: This is supported by the molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,D.

claim: The hub assembly may be destabilized as a consequence of the binding of just one or two regulatory segments.
source: Nevertheless, given the large distortions in the geometry of the hub with respect to the crystal structure, the hub assembly may be destabilized as a consequence of the binding of just one or two regulatory segments.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the simulation data.

claim: The binding of more than two regulatory segments to the hub would have to be accompanied by additional distortions and a loss of integrity of the hub assembly.
source: Alternatively, more than one regulatory segment might have to bind to promote disintegration of the hub. In the simulation, at interfaces where regulatory segments are not bound the interfacial grooves are constricted so that binding of the regulatory segments would be hindered substantially (Figure 6—figure supplement 3). This suggests that the binding of more than two regulatory segments to the hub would have to be accompanied by additional distortions and a loss of integrity of the hub assembly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the simulation data showing constricted grooves at non-docking interfaces.

claim: The rotation between the subunits that bracket the docking interfaces is much larger in the simulation than that observed in any crystal structures of the hub.
source: The rotation between the subunits that bracket the docking interfaces is much larger in the simulation than that observed in any crystal structures of the hub, including those with peptides bound at interfaces (Bhattacharyya et al., 2016; Chao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison between simulation data and previous crystal structures.

claim: In a structure of the hub assembly of CaMKII from Nematostella vectensis, the N-terminal portion of the linker preceding the hub folds back to interact with the hub.
source: In a structure of the hub assembly of CaMKII from the sea anemone Nematostella vectensis, the N-terminal portion of the linker preceding the hub folds back to interact with the hub (Bhattacharyya et al., 2016; Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous structural study and the figure.

claim: The N. vectensis hub assembly assumes a spiral, lock-washer conformation.
source: The N. vectensis hub assembly is slightly cracked, and it assumes a spiral, lock-washer conformation (Bhattacharyya et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous structural study.

claim: The interaction between the linker and the N. vectensis hub is likely to be an artefact of the low pH of crystallization and neutralization of acidic residues.
source: The interaction between the linker and the N. vectensis hub involves acidic residues in the linker interacting with acidic residues in the hub. This interaction is likely to be an artefact of the low pH of crystallization and neutralization of acidic residues (Bhattacharyya et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the crystallization conditions and the nature of the interactions.

claim: The interaction between the regulatory segment and the hub seen in the simulation involves favorable interactions between oppositely charged sidechains.
source: In contrast, the interaction between the regulatory segment and the hub seen in the simulation involves favorable interactions between oppositely charged sidechains.
evidence: This is supported by the molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: A very similar distortion is seen at both docking sites in the simulation, even though the register of the regulatory segment at one inter-subunit groove is offset by four residues with respect to the docking at the other inter-subunit groove.
source: It is striking that in the simulation a very similar distortion is seen at both docking sites, even though the register of the regulatory segment at one inter-subunit groove is offset by four residues with respect to the docking at the other inter-subunit groove (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The distortion at the two docking sites reflects an intrinsic feature of the hub dynamics, one that does not depend on the details of the interaction with the peptide.
source: This suggests that the distortion at the two docking sites reflects an intrinsic feature of the hub dynamics, one that does not depend on the details of the interaction with the peptide.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of distortions despite different binding registers.

claim: In a 6 µs simulation of the hub without the regulatory segments, the hub assembly showed large structural excursions at interfaces between hub domains.
source: In a 6 µs simulation of the hub without the regulatory segments, the hub assembly showed large structural excursions at interfaces between hub domains, including ones that are similar to those observed in the simulation of the hub with regulatory segments (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: There is a striking similarity between the displacement seen in the molecular dynamics simulation and that seen in the lowest-frequency internal modes from normal mode analysis.
source: We observed a striking similarity between the displacement seen in the molecular dynamics simulation and that seen in the lowest-frequency internal modes (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of molecular dynamics and normal mode analysis data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: In the lowest-frequency internal modes, two of the inter-subunit interfaces open, and the other interfaces close, just as in the molecular dynamics simulation.
source: In these normal modes, just as in the molecular dynamics simulation, two of the inter-subunit interfaces open, and the other interfaces close.
evidence: This is supported by the normal mode analysis data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The coupled opening of two interfaces and the correlated closing of the others is an intrinsic property of the hub assembly.
source: Thus, it appears that the coupled opening of two interfaces and the correlated closing of the others is an intrinsic property of the hub assembly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the normal mode analysis showing this behavior without regulatory segments.

claim: The regulatory segments take advantage of the opening of the interfaces to form stable interactions with the interfaces and trap this distorted structure.
source: In the molecular dynamics simulation, it appears that the regulatory segments take advantage of the opening of the interfaces to form stable interactions with the interfaces and trap this distorted structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the molecular dynamics simulation and normal mode analysis data.

claim: For unactivated mEGFP-CaMKII-α, the intensity distributions indicate the presence of a small population of monomers and dimers and a larger fraction of intact dodecameric holoenzymes.
source: For unactivated mEGFP-CaMKII-α, the intensity distributions indicate the presence of a small population of monomers and dimers and a larger fraction of intact dodecameric holoenzymes (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Upon activation of CaMKII-α, the peak that corresponds to smaller (monomeric and dimeric) CaMKII-α shows a ~1.3–2-fold increase in peak area.
source: There is a shift in the intensity distribution curve when compared to unactivated CaMKII-α, with the peak that corresponds to smaller (monomeric and dimeric) CaMKII-α showing a ~1.3–2-fold increase in peak area, indicating that upon activation some of the intact holoenzyme undergoes disassembly to form smaller oligomeric species.
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Upon activation, some of the intact holoenzyme undergoes disassembly to form smaller oligomeric species.
source: There is a shift in the intensity distribution curve when compared to unactivated CaMKII-α, with the peak that corresponds to smaller (monomeric and dimeric) CaMKII-α showing a ~1.3–2-fold increase in peak area, indicating that upon activation some of the intact holoenzyme undergoes disassembly to form smaller oligomeric species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the single-molecule TIRF microscopy data.

claim: The percentage of intermediate oligomeric species increases upon activation.
source: The percentage of intermediate oligomeric species also increases upon activation.
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Introduction of a mutation at the hub interface (F397A) leads to destabilization of the hub, with the release of dimers from the isolated hub.
source: Gel filtration experiments indicate that introduction of a mutation at the hub interface (F397A) leads to destabilization of the hub, with the release of dimers from the isolated hub (Bhattacharyya et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The unactivated sample of the F397A mutant has a much larger percentage of smaller species when compared to any of the wild-type samples.
source: The unactivated sample of this mutant form has a much larger percentage of smaller species when compared to any of the wild-type samples (Figure 9B, Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Upon activation of the F397A mutant, the peak corresponding to intact holoenzymes is no longer observed.
source: Upon activation, the peak corresponding to intact holoenzymes is no longer observed (Figure 9, Figure 9—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the activation leads to complete destabilization of the CaMKII F397A variant holoenzyme.
evidence: This is supported by the single-molecule TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Activation leads to complete destabilization of the CaMKII F397A variant holoenzyme.
source: Upon activation, the peak corresponding to intact holoenzymes is no longer observed (Figure 9, Figure 9—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the activation leads to complete destabilization of the CaMKII F397A variant holoenzyme.
evidence: This is an inference based on the single-molecule TIRF microscopy data.

claim: Efficient Thr 286 phosphorylation occurs only within a holoenzyme.
source: Efficient Thr 286 phosphorylation occurs only within a holoenzyme (De Koninck and Schulman, 1998), with the enzyme-kinase and substrate-kinase being tethered to the same hub at high local concentrations.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Subunit exchange provides a means for activated subunits to enter into holoenzymes that have not yet been activated and thereby produce more activated subunits by trans-phosphorylation.
source: This feature makes subunit exchange potentially important for spreading the activation of CaMKII, since it provides a means for activated subunits to enter into holoenzymes that have not yet been activated and thereby produce more activated subunits by trans-phosphorylation (Stratton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A CaMKII enzyme from choanoflagellates does not form stable oligomeric species, and it undergoes spontaneous subunit exchange.
source: Indeed, a CaMKII enzyme from choanoflagellates does not form stable oligomeric species, and it undergoes spontaneous subunit exchange (Bhattacharyya et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Mammalian CaMKII-α is very stable as a dodecameric or tetradecameric oligomer and it demonstrates an insignificant degree of subunit exchange when not activated.
source: In contrast, mammalian CaMKII-α is very stable as a dodecameric or tetradecameric oligomer and it demonstrates an insignificant degree of subunit exchange when not activated (Stratton et al., 2014; Bhattacharyya et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: If a CaMKII subunit undergoes phosphorylation at both Thr 286 and at Thr 305/Thr 306, then the regulatory segment might be released, and free to interact with the hub interface.
source: Thus, if a CaMKII subunit undergoes phosphorylation at both Thr 286 and at Thr 305/Thr 306, then the regulatory segment might be released, and free to interact with the hub interface.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on known phosphorylation effects.

claim: The local concentration of the regulatory segments with respect to the hub is estimated to be in the millimolar range.
source: The local concentration of the regulatory segments with respect to the hub is estimated to be in the millimolar range (Bhattacharyya et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The presentation of regulatory segment elements in cis to the hub could lead to rapid destabilization of the hub upon activation.
source: Given the observation that the addition of the regulatory segment peptides at micromolar concentrations in trans leads to hub disassembly, we conclude that the presentation of these elements in cis to the hub could lead to rapid destabilization of the hub upon activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mass spectrometry data and local concentration estimates.

claim: Subunit exchange in CaMKII has been proposed originally as a mechanism whereby the activation states of CaMKII could be maintained indefinitely, contributing to the storage of memories.
source: Subunit exchange in CaMKII has been proposed originally as a mechanism whereby the activation states of CaMKII could be maintained indefinitely, contributing to the storage of memories (Lisman, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous hypothesis.

claim: It is difficult to reconcile the memory storage mechanism with the action of phosphatases, which are expected to reset the activation states of CaMKII.
source: It is difficult to reconcile such a mechanism with the action of phosphatases, which are expected to reset the activation sates of CaMKII (Lee et al., 2009; Bhattacharyya et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is a critical evaluation supported by citations to studies on phosphatases.

claim: The destabilization of CaMKII holoenzymes upon activation is a mechanism that potentiates the effects of Ca2+ pulses under conditions when calmodulin is limiting.
source: Instead, we speculate that the destabilization of CaMKII holoenzymes upon activation is a mechanism that potentiates the effects of Ca2+ pulses under conditions when calmodulin is limiting, as is the case in neurons (Persechini and Stemmer, 2002; Pepke et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to studies on calmodulin availability.

claim: The release of dimers and other smaller oligomers can result in the spread of activated CaMKII species that can interact with and activate as yet unactivated holoenzymes.
source: Under these conditions, the release of dimers and other smaller oligomers can result in the spread of activated CaMKII species that can interact with and activate as yet unactivated holoenzymes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Approximately 30% of the GFP across all samples was found to be dark.
source: Approximately 30% of the GFP across all samples was found to be dark (Table 1), consistent with previous findings (Ulbrich and Isacoff, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Table 1 and citation to a previous study.
